items.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Terra, a midrange model with enhanced visual reasoning and computer use capabilities, priced at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Terra, a model designed to deliver fast and efficient performance with improved visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. Positioned as a midrange option in OpenAI's lineup, it targets tasks such as drafting proposals, interpreting technical drawings, filling out forms, and editing videos. GPT-6.1 Terra is priced at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, making it more affordable than higher-end models like GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol but more expensive than entry-level options such as GPT-6 Luna. The model aims to balance cost and performance, offering API developers and subscribers a practical choice for enhanced communication and faster computer-related tasks.

items.title: OpenAI announces new AI-generated proofs in mathematics, computer science, and physics and collaborates with academic communities to verify and build on results [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has released AI-generated research outputs addressing the Kakeya conjecture in mathematics, the Exponential Time Hypothesis in computer science, and quantum field theory in physics. The company is experimenting with different collaboration models involving external academic experts to validate and contextualize these findings while making materials publicly available or deferring release based on expert guidance. For the mathematics result, OpenAI published the AI's natural language proof and formalized Lean code openly, allowing researchers to independently explore the findings. For computer science and physics, OpenAI formed external groups to help explain and write up the results, with the physics group choosing to delay releasing AI-produced artifacts. These collaborations emphasize transparency, independence, and recognition without seeking academic credit, aiming to foster broader scientific understanding and community engagement around AI-generated research.

items.title: Cloudflare fixes cross-request KV cache data leak in GLM-5.3 Workers AI model affecting 155 responses with long prompts [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Cloudflare addressed a tenant isolation issue in its GLM-5.3 Workers AI model that caused data from other users' requests to appear in responses for prompts exceeding 681,280 tokens. The problem, reported by security researcher Gadi Evron, was caused by a misconfiguration and a bug in the open-source SGLang inference engine, leading to stale cache data being included in responses between August 27 and September 9, 2026. Cloudflare took the model offline promptly after confirming the issue, then remediated it by increasing the KV cache pool size to accommodate the full context window and patching the engine to safely handle rejected requests. The company confirmed no evidence of deliberate exploitation and has coordinated disclosure with SGLang maintainers while hardening its production deployments to prevent similar bugs.

items.title: Greptile uses GPT-6 Astra to automate application testing beyond code review, integrates Daybreak for security, and employs Codex to reduce code rework [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Greptile builds AI agents that review and test code changes with full context of the codebase, aiming to reduce bugs and improve software reliability. The company uses GPT-6 Astra to simulate user workflows and test application behavior at scale, enabling automated detection of issues like UI problems that static code review might miss. In addition to testing, Greptile integrates Daybreak to enhance security defenses against increasingly sophisticated attacks, making advanced protection accessible even to startups. The company also leverages Codex connected to its knowledge base to generate code that aligns with existing patterns, reducing rework and improving development efficiency. Greptile plans to accelerate software development further with its Ultrafast initiative, aiming to streamline the process of changing and shipping critical enterprise software.

items.title: Anthropic files S-1 for IPO revealing $16.3B H1 2026 revenue, $80.7B GAAP loss, and $518B in multi-year cloud commitments to Google, AWS, and Microsoft [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic filed its Form S-1 registration statement for a proposed Nasdaq IPO, disclosing rapid revenue growth to $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026 alongside an $80.7 billion GAAP net loss largely due to non-cash revaluations. The filing also revealed $518 billion in non-cancellable cloud purchase commitments spanning Google Cloud, AWS, and Microsoft Azure through the next decade, highlighting extensive vendor financing and infrastructure lock-in within the AI industry. The S-1 footnotes detail how Anthropic's cloud commitments include $111 billion to Google Cloud, $110 billion to AWS, and up to $45 billion to Microsoft Azure, with nearly 80% structured as take-or-pay contracts. Additionally, nearly half of Anthropic's 2025 revenue flowed through cloud marketplaces like AWS Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI, where distribution fees of about 16% are charged before Anthropic pays for the underlying hardware. These financial arrangements illustrate a circular capital flow among major tech companies involved in AI development and deployment.

items.title: Anthropic files 335-page IPO prospectus outlining its AI technology and risks amid debate over its role and trustworthiness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus, a detailed 335-page document that includes extensive discussion of risks and presents the company's perspective on its AI technology and its potential impact. The filing follows weeks of speculation and highlights Anthropic's narrative about the singularity and the unique capabilities of its AI systems. The company has cultivated a complex public image, portraying itself as both a leader in AI safety and a profit-driven enterprise valued at over $1.5 trillion. This dual identity raises questions about its motivations and trustworthiness, especially as it advocates for responsible AI development while competing in a high-stakes industry. Anthropic's cofounders and executives have made public statements emphasizing the mysterious and potentially dangerous nature of their technology, contributing to ongoing debates about AI regulation and oversight.

items.title: Police increasingly pull over drivers flagged by AI for 'suspicious' travel patterns using automated license plate reader data [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: In 2025, Grace Knowles was pulled over by an FBI agent who cited AI surveillance of her license plate and travel patterns as suspicious, despite her normal driving. The officer showed her a heat map of her movements generated by AI analyzing automated license plate reader (ALPR) data, illustrating how law enforcement uses this technology to flag and stop drivers. This case highlights the growing use of AI-driven license plate surveillance by companies like Flock, which law enforcement agencies employ to identify potentially suspicious travel behavior. The expansion of such AI tools raises concerns about innocent drivers being stopped based on algorithmic assessments without clear explanations or transparency.

items.title: Anthropic files for IPO to raise up to $100 billion, Meta plans $95 billion stock offering, and SpaceX secures $40 billion GPU financing deal amid intensifying AI funding competition [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic, SpaceX, and Meta Platforms have announced major fundraising efforts to support their AI projects, potentially raising nearly $235 billion collectively. Anthropic filed for an IPO aiming to raise up to $100 billion, Meta plans to raise $95 billion through stock offerings, and SpaceX secured a $40 billion GPU financing deal, the largest ever. These moves increase competition for capital, potentially impacting smaller AI companies. In related developments, Microsoft announced a voluntary buyout offer for up to 60,000 employees, and DoorDash is reportedly in advanced talks to acquire Instacart for $17 billion. Additionally, a cybersecurity startup named Cathedral reportedly accessed Anthropic's internal systems using AI agents. Industry experts highlight growing scrutiny over AI investments due to limited financial returns outside the tech sector.

items.title: OpenAI announces three major scientific discoveries in math, computer science, and physics with external academic collaboration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has revealed three significant scientific findings involving mathematics, computer science, and physics, marking a shift in its approach by collaborating with external experts called "shepherds" to guide and validate the results. The discoveries include a proof related to the Euclidean wave equation, a refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis in computer science, and a rigorous existence proof for certain quantum field theories in physics. For the computer science discovery, a group of experts including original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis will examine and explain the proof, with materials released publicly on GitHub. In mathematics, OpenAI released AI-generated outputs for researchers to analyze independently. The physics results are being shepherded by a team of prominent physicists. OpenAI also issued an open letter seeking community input on norms for handling AI-generated scientific breakthroughs and early access to such results.

items.title: Sebastian Raschka releases an 11-hour video course on building reasoning models from scratch using Python and PyTorch [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Sebastian Raschka has published a comprehensive video course totaling over 11 hours that teaches how to build reasoning models from the ground up. The course covers key topics such as evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, using Python and PyTorch with a focus on a pre-trained Qwen3 model. The videos serve as a sequel to Raschka's previous course on building large language models and are designed for learners comfortable with Python and PyTorch. The course emphasizes practical coding and understanding of reasoning models, which are essential components powering modern AI agents and large language models with enhanced problem-solving capabilities.

Candidates analyze how AI interprets and prioritizes information to optimize their messaging for these models, aiming to influence voter perceptions more effectively. This development highlights the increasing integration of AI technologies in political campaigns and the potential impact on democratic processes.

items.title: AI agent builds complete game directly in WebAssembly, bypassing traditional software stack layers designed for human programmers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A recent experiment demonstrated that an AI agent named Claude Code can write an entire turn-based strategy game, HarvestChain, directly in WebAssembly text format without using higher-level programming languages or frameworks. This approach eliminates many layers of the traditional software stack, which exist primarily to accommodate human limitations in coding and collaboration. The game includes a simulation, 3D renderer, interface, input handling, saving, and other features all within a single compact module of about 40 KB compressed, significantly smaller than typical web games. The AI completed the project in a few hours, highlighting how AI can bypass abstractions designed for humans, potentially leading to more efficient and compact software for specific use cases.

items.title: CodeRabbit uses GPT-6.1 Sol to enhance security analysis across complex codebases, linking behavior across files and dependencies [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: CodeRabbit integrates GPT-6.1 Sol as the core model in its security agent to investigate potential vulnerabilities across complex codebases, extending review beyond individual code changes. The system analyzes pull requests, dependencies, and linked repositories to identify security risks and supports developers by flagging issues within existing workflows. The platform also offers exploit verification in isolated sandboxes and can draft proposed fixes for human review and approval. This approach helps teams understand broader security implications while keeping human reviewers responsible for final decisions on code changes.

items.title: Anthropic warns in IPO filing that its AI data centers rely heavily on natural gas amid rising costs and supply constraints [ * ] [ ◼ ]

The filing highlights intense competition for power supply and suitable data center locations, with some planned facilities using on-site natural gas turbines. The company acknowledges that climate change, driven in part by fossil fuel use, could increase its operating costs due to higher electricity and cooling expenses. Anthropic also notes that regulatory actions, infrastructure costs, and limited gas pipeline capacity could delay or force cancellation of data center projects, potentially hindering its growth and ability to scale AI compute infrastructure.

items.title: The Argument in Favor of Tranched Rounds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Before we get to today's column, the big day is here: Anthropic dropped its long-awaited public S-1 filing Monday morning. Tune in today for stories from my colleagues and me that will be breaking down the most important takeaways from the filing, such as improvements in the company's compute efficiency, details on its spending and cash burn, and interesting new disclosures that could point to an eventual end to its unusual Long-Term Benefit Trust, a group of non-shareholders who advise the company on safety and social issues and can appoint a majority of its board. Onto today's column... It seems like every AI startup financing these days has multiple tranches in which different investors get in at different valuations. At first, it was unusual to see just two tranches. Now we see extra-hot funding rounds with three tranches or more. It's no secret that investors aren't thrilled about these multi-tranche rounds (specifically, the investors that can't get in at the lower valuation). Some of them argue that the practice allows bigger venture capital firms to flex their power and force smaller VC firms into the second, more expensive tranche. They also say it allows the startup to claim a bigger valuation, even though some or most of the new capital came in at a lower price. But founders and many investors tell me that the unique capital needs of AI companies, which are eternally starved of enough servers, is driving these unusual structures.

The reason for their apprehension: Stripe in many cases is enabling AI agent purchases through virtual cards for one-time use, which can leave card networks with less control over the shopping and payment process, people who work closely with the card firms say. Mastercard and Visa have developed their own payment technology for agent shopping that would use customers' existing cards, giving the card companies more visibility into who's making what purchases. That method is still at an early stage, though.
